newsitem.title: USA: NYC's debt gets higher rating from European agency.
newsitem.headline: NYC's debt gets higher rating from European agency.

text.p: New York City on Thursday said European rating agency IBCA gave its general obligation bonds a higher rating than any domestic rating agency, assigning a single-A grade.

A New York City official, who declined to be named, said IBCA, known for rating sovereign and corporate debt, cited the city's strong financial outlook, as well as the high degree of comfort afforded by the way property taxes first are funneled through the state comptroller.

"The rating reflects the city's currently robust finances," said IBCA in a statement provided by the city official. The rating agency also said, "We're particularly comforted by provisions imposed on the city to ensure the prompt and certain payment of debt service."

New York City's GOs have a first claim on all city revenues, and the city has an unlimited right to levy the real estate tax to repay the debt, IBCA said. Further, real estate taxes are paid directly to a debt service fund maintained by the state comptroller.

The European rating agency gave the city's short-term foreign issues a slightly higher rating of A1. New York City is one of the few U.S. municipalities that sells its debt overseas. IBCA's ratings affect about $32 billion of debt that the city has outstanding.
The city official said that Standard & Poor's Corp rates New York City at BBB+, and Moody's Investors Service Baa1, and Fitch Investors Service at A-minus.

On the plus side, IBCA said the city had rebuilt its service industries--from media to tourism--and made substantial improvements since its image was battered by high crime and other woes. "The inner city and other economic and social problems, particularly crime, which were thought to typify the city by many people, especially in the 1970s, now are in retreat, if not yet defeated," IBCA added immigration was offsetting a middle-class flight to the suburbs, revitalizing the city.

While New York City's ability to balance its budget--as required by law--over the past 16 years was applauded, the rating agency questioned the city's high debt service costs, though it said the city's infrastructure would suffer without the capital program. "The main negative factor in the rating is the extent of, and rise in, the city's debt." Later, it added: "The prospective debt and debt service ratios appear sustainable although they are undoubtedly high."
